title: Amelia Hart (librarian)
biography_text:
Amelia Rose Hart (born 12 March 1984) is a community Librarian known for developing inclusive cataloging practices and neighborhood-based reading services in the fictional city of Merrowfield. She has worked as a Librarian in public libraries, school libraries, and a small prison library unit, while maintaining her primary role and identity as a Librarian. Her work focuses on making library collections easier to understand for readers with different language levels and learning needs.

Hart was born in the riverside district of East Merrowfield to a postal clerk and a bus mechanic. She attended local public schools and often visited the Merrowfield Central Library, where she received her first library card at age seven. During secondary school, she volunteered in the school library, shelving books and helping other students locate materials. Her early experiences with classification systems and reference tools influenced her decision to become a Librarian.

After completing secondary education, Hart studied information science at Merrowfield Civic College, a regional institution. She later earned a bachelor’s degree in Library and Information Services from Northbridge Open University through part-time distance study. While studying, she worked as a library assistant at the Merrowfield Central Library. In this support role, she performed circulation tasks, checked in returned materials, and observed the daily responsibilities of professional Librarians. She decided to qualify as a Librarian and took additional certification courses in cataloging, youth services, and digital literacy.

Hart was appointed as a full-time Librarian at the Merrowfield East Branch Library in 2010. As a Librarian, she managed the branch’s small reference collection, organized the nonfiction shelves, and oversaw borrowing records. She also designed subject guides for students in middle school and early secondary school, using simplified language and visual symbols. These guides explained how to use the catalog, how to understand call numbers, and how to evaluate basic information sources. Her approach aimed to keep the library catalog accurate while also making it more accessible.

In 2014, Hart transferred to the Merrowfield West Learning Hub, a joint facility shared by a public library and a nearby middle school. She retained her position as a Librarian and was responsible for both public and school collections in the same building. She coordinated with teachers to align library materials with classroom topics, but she continued to work under the library department and not the school staff. Her duties as a Librarian included maintaining the online catalog, selecting age-appropriate materials, and training student helpers in basic shelving and labeling.

Hart developed a color-coded label system for the youth nonfiction section. Instead of replacing standard classification numbers, she added colored icons to the book spines to show broad subjects such as science, history, arts, and technology. This system was tested in the Merrowfield West Learning Hub and later adopted in several other branches in the city. The system was intended to support readers who found traditional numeric classification confusing, while still preserving the structure needed by Librarians for collection management.

During 2017, Hart accepted a temporary assignment as a Librarian for the Merrowfield Community Reintegration Center, a small correctional facility. She remained employed by the city library service and continued to be classified and paid as a Librarian. At the center, she reorganized a neglected book room into a functioning library space. She created a simple catalog on paper index cards, introduced a basic borrowing system, and labeled materials by reading level. Her work focused on informational texts, health resources, and vocational manuals. When the temporary project ended, she returned to public library branch service.

In 2019, Hart became the lead Librarian at the newly opened Merrowfield Riverside Library, a medium-sized branch designed to combine physical collections with digital access points. As lead Librarian, she supervised a small team of library assistants and part-time clerks. Her responsibilities included selecting print and digital materials, maintaining catalog accuracy, and managing the branch budget for collections. She also coordinated with the city’s information technology department to ensure that public computers and online catalog terminals functioned reliably.

Hart’s work as a Librarian has emphasized clear organization and user-focused catalog design. She helped draft a plain-language glossary of library terms for Merrowfield Library Service, explaining expressions such as "circulation", "hold", "renewal", and "interlibrary loan". The glossary was integrated into printed bookmarks and the city’s library website. She also piloted short, repeated orientation sessions where new users learned how to search the catalog and locate items on shelves using step-by-step guides.

Hart has participated in regional workshops for Librarians, where she has presented case studies about color-coded labels and simplified subject headings for younger readers. She has contributed practical examples to internal training manuals, including sample catalog records and shelf maps. These materials have been used to train new Librarians and library assistants in Merrowfield. She has not published books, but her internal documents and presentations have circulated within the regional library network.

Outside her formal duties, Hart continues to engage with professional development as a Librarian. She completes online courses about metadata standards, digital preservation, and accessibility in library services. She has shown particular interest in how screen readers interact with online catalogs and how font choices affect readability for users with visual processing differences. She has advocated within staff meetings for consistent alt text descriptions on library websites and for testing catalog interfaces with actual users before major updates.

Hart remains employed as a Librarian at the Merrowfield Riverside Library. Her ongoing work includes monitoring borrowing trends, adjusting collection priorities, and updating subject guides to reflect new areas of interest, such as climate science and basic programming. She continues to focus on the practical tasks of a Librarian: organizing information, maintaining accurate records, and supporting independent learning for a wide range of readers in her community.

Her practice centers on rendering library collections more intelligible for readers who possess diverse language proficiencies and varied cognitive or learning needs.

She attended local public schools and frequently visited the Merrowfield Central Library, where she obtained her first library card at age seven. During secondary school, she volunteered in the school library, carrying out shelving duties and assisting fellow students in locating materials. These early encounters with classification systems, reference tools, and the practical organization of knowledge significantly shaped her decision to pursue professional qualification as a Librarian.

After completing her secondary education, Hart studied information science at Merrowfield Civic College, a regional tertiary institution. She subsequently earned a bachelor’s degree in Library and Information Services from Northbridge Open University through part-time distance learning. While undertaking these studies, she worked as a library assistant at the Merrowfield Central Library. In this subordinate but formative role, she handled circulation operations, checked in returned materials, and closely observed the day-to-day responsibilities of professional Librarians. Motivated by this exposure, she resolved to qualify formally as a Librarian and completed additional certification courses in cataloging, youth services, and digital literacy.

Hart received her first appointment as a full-time Librarian at the Merrowfield East Branch Library in 2010. In this capacity as a Librarian, she managed the branch’s compact reference collection, organized the nonfiction shelving sequence, and monitored borrowing records. She also designed subject guides for middle school and early secondary students, employing simplified language and visual symbols. These guides clarified how to use the catalog, interpret call numbers, and evaluate basic information sources. Her strategy sought to preserve catalog accuracy and professional standards while simultaneously enhancing accessibility for novice and struggling readers.

In 2014, Hart transferred to the Merrowfield West Learning Hub, a joint facility that integrates a public library with a nearby middle school in a shared building. She retained her status and duties as a Librarian and assumed responsibility for both the public and school collections housed in the same space. She coordinated with classroom teachers to align library resources with curricular topics, yet she continued to operate under the public library department rather than as part of the school’s instructional staff. Her Librarian responsibilities encompassed maintaining the online catalog, selecting age-appropriate materials, and training student volunteers in fundamental shelving, labeling, and basic library procedures.

At the Merrowfield West Learning Hub, Hart developed a color-coded labeling system for the youth nonfiction section. Rather than abolishing or substituting the established numeric classification scheme, she added colored icons to the spines of books to denote broad subject domains such as science, history, arts, and technology. This hybrid system, which preserved the underlying classification numbers, was initially piloted at the Learning Hub and subsequently adopted by several other branches in Merrowfield. It was explicitly intended to assist readers who found traditional numeric classification confusing, while still maintaining the structural rigor required by Librarians for collection management and catalog integrity.

In 2017, Hart accepted a temporary assignment as a Librarian at the Merrowfield Community Reintegration Center, a small correctional facility. During this period she remained an employee of the city library service and continued to be classified, supervised, and remunerated as a Librarian rather than as correctional or teaching staff. At the center, she transformed a neglected book room into a functioning library environment. She created a simple catalog using paper index cards, instituted a basic borrowing system, and labeled materials according to reading level. Her collection development emphasized informational texts, health resources, and vocational manuals that could support reintegration and practical skill-building. When the temporary project concluded, she returned to service in the public library branches.

In 2019, Hart was appointed lead Librarian at the newly established Merrowfield Riverside Library, a medium-sized branch designed to integrate traditional physical collections with extensive digital access points. As lead Librarian, she supervised a small team of library assistants and part-time clerks. Her responsibilities included selecting both print and digital materials, ensuring catalog accuracy, and managing the branch budget allocated for collections. She also coordinated with the city’s information technology department to maintain reliable operation of public computers and online catalog terminals.

Across these roles, Hart’s work as a Librarian has emphasized systematic organization and user-centered catalog design. She helped draft a plain-language glossary of library terminology for the Merrowfield Library Service, clarifying expressions such as “circulation,” “hold,” “renewal,” and “interlibrary loan.” This glossary was incorporated into printed bookmarks and integrated into the city’s library website. She also piloted brief, repeated orientation sessions in which new users learned how to search the catalog and locate items on shelves through step-by-step guides and demonstrations.

Hart has participated in regional workshops for Librarians, where she has presented case studies on the implementation of color-coded labels and on simplified subject headings for younger readers. She has contributed applied examples to internal training manuals, including model catalog records, annotated shelf maps, and procedural checklists. These internal materials have been used to train newly appointed Librarians and library assistants throughout Merrowfield. Although she has not authored commercially published books, her internal documentation and professional presentations circulate within the regional library network as practical training resources.

Beyond her formal job description, Hart continues to pursue professional development as a Librarian. She completes online courses on metadata standards, digital preservation practices, and accessibility in library services. She has shown particular interest in how screen readers interact with online catalogs and how typography and font choices influence readability for users with visual processing differences. Within staff meetings, she has advocated for consistent and descriptive alt text for images on library websites and for systematically testing catalog interfaces with actual users prior to major software updates.

Hart remains employed as a Librarian at the Merrowfield Riverside Library. Her ongoing responsibilities include monitoring borrowing trends, adjusting collection priorities, and revising subject guides to address emerging areas of interest, such as climate science and introductory computer programming. She continues to concentrate on the core practical tasks of a Librarian: organizing information, maintaining accurate and reliable records, and supporting independent learning for a wide spectrum of readers in her community.
